chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from al-Husayn ibn Uthman and Muhammad ibn Abi Hamza, from Is'haq ibn Ammar and others, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the man who emancipates his slave and marries him to his daughter, and stipulates a condition upon him that if he were to wrong/deceive her, he would be returned to slavery. He said: His stipulation stands.

key_terms.أَغَارَهَا: To deceive or wrong her; to harm or betray her trust.
key_terms.الرِّق: Bondage, slavery, the state of being enslaved.
key_terms.شَرْط: Condition, stipulation, prerequisite attached to a legal contract.
key_terms.مَمْلُوك: An owned slave/serf; literally 'one who is owned.' In classical Islamic law, refers to a person held in bondage.
key_terms.يَشْتَرِط: To stipulate a condition; to attach a prerequisite to a legal act.
key_terms.يُزَوِّج: To give in marriage; for a guardian to arrange the marriage of a ward.
key_terms.يُعْتِق: To emancipate, set free from slavery. A meritorious act in Islamic law.

ai.seo_question: Can a master stipulate conditions when emancipating a slave and giving him his daughter in marriage?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses a specific legal scenario in which a master frees his slave, gives him his daughter in marriage, but places a contractual condition on the freedom: if the former slave mistreats or deceives his wife, he reverts to slavery. Imam al-Sadiq rules that such a stipulation is valid and enforceable. In early Islamic jurisprudence, conditional emancipation clauses were debated, and this hadith provides a Shia legal precedent affirming that freedom can be coupled with protective conditions for the emancipated person's family.
